newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina seen setting reasonable 1997 budget goal.
newsitem.headline: Argentina seen setting reasonable 1997 budget goal.

text.p: Argentina's Economy Minister Roque Fernandez has set realistic goals for the country's 1997 budget unveiled last Friday -- a welcome departure from the rosy fiscal scenarios presented by his predecessor, economic analysts said.
"This budget has more modest objectives than those (former Economy Minister Domingo) Cavallo used to come up with in the past," said economist Ines Piccinino at Asesores Economicos consultants.
"It's a good thing Fernandez did not present a budget with goals impossible to meet. That would have had a negative reception in times when the economic plan is increasinglingly unpopular."
Cavallo was known for forecasting rosy scenarios that had to be watered down throughout the fiscal year.
The 1997 budget proposal makes a reasonable five percent growth assumption for the year but is overly optimistic in its expected 15 percent growth in fiscal revenues, analysts said.

The budget estimates a 4.3 percent rise in consumption, a 10 percent rise in investment and a foreign trade deficit of $2.0 billion with a 10 percent rise in imports and a seven percent rise in exports.
The government also expects a fiscal deficit of $3.04 billion, equal to one percent of the country's gross domestic product and substantially lower than this year's $5.0 billion.
The government said that a third of the fiscal gap is a result of the transfer of pension funds from the provinces to the federal government, which will account for about $1.0 billion.
"One could say that this budget is the transition towards a structurally balanced budget in 1998," said the government.
But analysts warn that some public accounts might be a bit on the optimistic side.

"In general the budget is reasonably well thought out, but we believe the government will get some $500 million less than it expects in revenue even though we are estimating six rather that five percent growth," said economist Nicolas Dujovne at Macroeconomica consultants.
The government expects revenues to grow by 15 percent to $25.6 billion, or an 11.3 percent growth to $41.0 billion if social security contributions are included.
Fernandez said that the rise in revenue will be a result of growth, improved tax collection -- the wealth tax in particular -- and a rise in the price of fuels and income tax.
At $43.0 billion, expenditures will rise 0.2 percent despite the so-called Second Reform of State that will help save $1.3 billion from streamlining the public administration.
The rise in expenditures will be a result of increased payments on public debt.
Analyst say that with a $3.0 billion deficit and $9.0 billion in debt payments next year, the government will have to seek $12.0 billion in local and international financing.
"The fiscal deficit does not worry me...but the level of indebtedness is something to be concerned of. It will be four times the size of exports," said economist Marcelo Lascano.
"You have to keep in mind that the World Bank gets concerned once debt doubles the size of exports," he said.
